attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post. It follows his line about errors in mission-critical systems.

semantics.note: An observation about Amazon now. 'AI-generated code' is a bit narrower than his wording, which refers to errors from AI coding systems. The context implies that reading but does not state it. 'Deadly' is rhetorical.

contract.note: The plain reading counts errors from AI coding tools, including AI advice that engineers acted on. That is a fair, ordinary reading. It is broader than the normalised 'AI-generated code', and that difference drives the result.

evidence.note: The FT reports Amazon's internal note. It tied a trend of high-blast-radius incidents partly to GenAI-assisted changes and novel GenAI use.

Company disclosure. It denies any AI-written code, which goes against the narrow proposition. But it concedes one outage in which an engineer followed inaccurate AI advice, which partly supports the contract's reading.
Shows the early-March retail outages were large. It does not say which outage, if any, involved AI tools.

reviews.rationale: What holds: AI coding tools were tied to outages in Amazon's critical retail systems. Amazon's internal note names GenAI-assisted changes as a factor, and Amazon admits one outage involved bad AI advice. What doesn't hold: the specific 'AI-generated code' part. Amazon denies it (a company claim) and no independent source confirms it. The harm from the one AI-linked outage is also not public.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post, citing the FT report.

semantics.note: An observation that big problems from AI coding tools have arrived. 'As he predicted' is self-vindication. His earlier warnings were about maintenance and security, which differ from the Amazon incidents.

contract.note: Reading 'big' as real customer or business impact, and requiring AI to be a real contributing factor, is fair and ordinary. Whether that is met depends on trusting Amazon's internal documents or its public rebuttal.

evidence.note: Amazon's internal note, as the FT reports it, links high-blast-radius incidents to GenAI-assisted changes and lists novel GenAI use among the contributing factors.
Fortune reports the internal document first named GenAI-assisted changes as a factor in incidents back to Q3, then the reference was deleted.
Company disclosure. Only one incident involved AI tooling, no AI-written code, and Amazon calls the cause user error rather than AI.
December AWS Kiro incident. FT sources say it was a 13-hour interruption. Amazon calls it limited and blames user error. How big it was is disputed.

reviews.rationale: What holds: production incidents tied to AI coding tools had begun by March 2026. Amazon's internal documents and its public concession of one AI-advice outage both show this. What is unsettled: whether AI was a real cause of big incidents. Amazon disputes it, and no neutral root-cause analysis exists. The fit to his earlier maintenance and security predictions is also loose.
